prompt: A 54-year-old courier collapsed beside his delivery van and does not respond, while your partner squeezes a bag-mask over his face. Which finding shows those breaths are reaching the lungs?

options.text: The chest wall visibly rises with each squeeze
The pulse oximeter number climbs within a few seconds
The bag feels tighter as each breath is delivered
The abdomen rises and falls with each squeeze

explanation: On this unresponsive courier, chest-wall movement is the immediate bedside check that bagged air is entering the lungs. A saturation number lags by a minute or more, a stiffer bag suggests obstruction or poor compliance, and a rising abdomen means the breath went into the stomach.

distractorExplanations.b: Pulse oximetry lags ventilation and can be misled by poor perfusion, so a quick climb is not proof these squeezes are landing.
distractorExplanations.c: Rising resistance means obstruction, gastric distension, or stiff lungs, which is the opposite of a breath that is moving easily into the chest.
distractorExplanations.d: Abdominal rise means the breath is inflating the stomach, usually from too much volume or a poor airway position.

prompt: You find a sweaty 29-year-old on a bathroom floor with pinpoint pupils, six shallow respirations a minute, and a used fentanyl patch on the arm. Once the mouth is open, what do you do about those six shallow breaths?

options.text: Roll him on his side and watch without assisting breaths
Ventilate with a bag-mask and consider naloxone
Give naloxone and wait for breathing to return on its own
Put a nonrebreather on him at 15 liters per minute

explanation: Six shallow breaths and a fentanyl patch mean hypoventilation is the immediate threat, so bag-mask ventilation starts now while naloxone is prepared. The antagonist takes time, and a mask that only enriches inspired gas cannot move air for someone breathing this poorly.

distractorExplanations.a: The recovery position is for a person who is already breathing adequately. Six shallow breaths a minute still need assistance.
distractorExplanations.c: Naloxone does not restore ventilation instantly. Waiting on the drug leaves this hypoventilation untreated for those minutes.
distractorExplanations.d: A nonrebreather needs adequate spontaneous breathing. It cannot replace breaths that are this slow and shallow.

prompt: A 67-year-old with pneumonia is awake, speaking in short phrases, and pulling air without assistance, yet the saturation sits at 86 percent on room air. Which device gives him the highest inspired oxygen fraction?

options.text: Nasal cannula flowing at 6 liters per minute
Simple face mask flowing at 10 liters per minute
Nonrebreather at 15 liters per minute
Venturi mask locked at 28 percent oxygen

explanation: This man is still breathing, so the device with a reservoir and one-way valves, run fast enough that the bag stays inflated, delivers a higher inspired fraction than a cannula, a simple mask, or a Venturi locked at 28 percent.

distractorExplanations.a: A nasal cannula at 6 liters per minute tops out near 44 percent, well below a reservoir mask.
distractorExplanations.b: A simple face mask mixes room air through side ports and typically lands around 35 to 60 percent.
distractorExplanations.d: A Venturi mask at 28 percent is a fixed low concentration, chosen when a precise modest dose is the goal.

prompt: At a picnic, a 6-year-old develops a harsh high-pitched noise on inspiration, tugs at the base of the neck, and drools slightly after a bee sting. Where is that noise coming from?

options.text: Narrowed bronchi from acute bronchospasm
Fluid-filled alveoli of left heart failure
A normal childhood sound needing no care
Partial obstruction above the vocal cords

explanation: A harsh inspiratory noise plus neck tugging after a sting is swelling above the vocal cords, and that opening can close further. Bronchospasm whistles on exhalation, alveolar fluid crackles, and this sound is not a normal childhood noise.

distractorExplanations.a: Bronchospasm produces an expiratory wheeze from the lower airways, not a harsh inspiratory noise with neck tugging.
distractorExplanations.b: Fluid in the alveoli causes crackles. It does not make a high-pitched inspiratory sound at the neck.
distractorExplanations.c: This inspiratory noise is a warning of upper-airway narrowing. It is not a sound children make when the airway is healthy.

prompt: Thick vomit fills the mouth of an intoxicated 40-year-old, and you have a rigid catheter ready. How long may each suction pass run before you pause so he can be oxygenated?

options.text: Limit each pass to about 15 seconds
Keep suctioning until the mouth is dry
Apply suction while the catheter advances
Allow a full minute of suction each pass

explanation: Each adult suction pass stays near 15 seconds because the catheter is pulling oxygen out along with the vomit. You insert without suction, aspirate on the way out, then ventilate or oxygenate before another pass. Drying the mouth is not the goal.

distractorExplanations.b: Suctioning until the mouth is dry keeps oxygen from reaching the lungs for far too long and is not required to clear a working airway.
distractorExplanations.c: Suction is applied while the catheter is withdrawn. Suction during insertion grabs tissue and does not clear the pool of vomit.
distractorExplanations.d: A full minute of suction is long enough to cause serious hypoxia. Adult passes are kept near 15 seconds.

prompt: Ejected from a rollover, an unresponsive driver is snoring, and a bystander tells you to tip the head back and lift the chin. Why is that head position a poor default?

options.text: It drives the tongue backward and occludes the pharynx
It extends the neck and can worsen a cervical injury
It sharply raises pressure inside the skull
It opens the airway less well than a jaw thrust

explanation: This ejected driver may have an unstable cervical spine, and tipping the head back extends the neck. The maneuver actually lifts the tongue off the posterior pharynx. It is set aside here because of spinal motion, not because it fails to open the airway or because it raises intracranial pressure.

distractorExplanations.a: Head-tilt with chin-lift lifts the tongue forward. The hazard in this rollover is neck extension, not pushing the tongue back.
distractorExplanations.c: The reason to skip this maneuver is movement of an injured cervical spine, not a rise in intracranial pressure.
distractorExplanations.d: Head-tilt and chin-lift usually open the airway well. It is avoided after this ejection because of the neck, not because a jaw thrust works better in general.

prompt: Sitting forward, a longtime smoker produces a musical whistling sound on exhalation, with a prolonged expiratory phase that eases after a bronchodilator. Which structures are narrowed?

options.text: A trachea so blocked that no air moves
Swollen tissue at the level of the larynx
Bronchi tightened by lower-airway spasm
Air under pressure in the pleural space

explanation: A musical sound on the way out, with a long expiratory phase that eases after a bronchodilator, comes from tightened bronchi. A plugged trachea moves no air, laryngeal swelling is harsh on inspiration, and pleural air quiets one side rather than whistling.

distractorExplanations.a: Complete tracheal blockage moves no air, so there is no musical sound to hear on exhalation.
distractorExplanations.b: Swelling at the larynx produces a harsh inspiratory sound, not an expiratory whistle that eases with a bronchodilator.
distractorExplanations.d: Air in the pleural space quiets breath sounds on the affected side. It does not whistle through narrowed bronchi.

prompt: A nursing-home resident is awake yet breathing eight shallow times a minute, with little chest excursion and a saturation of 84 percent. What corrects the shallow breathing?

options.text: Oxygen by nasal cannula and no assisted breaths
Oxygen by nonrebreather and no assisted breaths
Abdominal thrusts until the rate picks up
Bag-mask breaths that move air into the lungs

explanation: Eight shallow breaths a minute are not moving enough air, so oxygen flowing across the face cannot fix the minute ventilation. This resident needs positive-pressure breaths. Abdominal thrusts are for a foreign body, which is not what the shallow rate shows.

distractorExplanations.a: A nasal cannula enriches inspired gas only when the person is already breathing well enough. It does not correct a rate of eight shallow breaths.
distractorExplanations.b: A nonrebreather also depends on adequate spontaneous breathing. It cannot supply the tidal volume this resident is missing.
distractorExplanations.c: Abdominal thrusts are for a conscious person with a complete foreign-body obstruction, not for hypoventilation without choking.

prompt: Gasping awake at midnight, a retired teacher coughs up pink frothy sputum, has crackles at both bases, a blood pressure of 168/96, and a saturation of 88 percent, and he follows commands. Which device should you reach for?

options.text: CPAP while he is awake with fluid-filled lungs
Abdominal thrusts for a tracheal foreign body
Bag ventilation for someone who stopped breathing
A supraglottic airway for an unprotected airway

explanation: Pink frothy sputum, bilateral crackles, hypertension, and an alert teacher who follows commands describe cardiogenic edema. Continuous positive pressure can stent fluid-filled alveoli when he is awake, protecting his airway, and protocol allows it. He is not apneic, choking, or unprotected.

distractorExplanations.b: Nothing in this midnight picture is a tracheal foreign body. Abdominal thrusts do not move alveolar fluid.
distractorExplanations.c: He is gasping and following commands, so he has spontaneous breathing. Bag ventilation is for inadequate or absent breaths.
distractorExplanations.d: He follows commands and is protecting his airway. A supraglottic airway is for failed ventilation in a patient who cannot protect it.

prompt: After an hour short of breath on a high trail, a hiker who first looked pale now has blue lips and a blue tongue. What does the blue tongue tell you?

options.text: Carbon monoxide saturation of his hemoglobin
A late sign of serious hypoxemia
Severe anemia with a normal saturation
Dilated skin vessels from a warm environment

explanation: Blue lips and a blue tongue after an hour of breathlessness are central cyanosis, which appears only after a substantial amount of hemoglobin is desaturated. It is a late finding, so this hiker needs oxygen now rather than reassurance that the color is early, cosmetic, or unrelated to oxygen.

distractorExplanations.a: Carbon monoxide poisoning tends toward cherry-red skin, and the pulse oximeter can look falsely reassuring. It does not produce a blue tongue.
distractorExplanations.c: Severe anemia looks pale. Cyanosis needs enough desaturated hemoglobin to show, so anemia often hides the blue color rather than causing it.
distractorExplanations.d: Warm dilated vessels flush the skin red. A blue tongue reflects desaturated hemoglobin, not heat.

prompt: Mid-attack, a college student's noisy exhalation has gone quiet, accessory muscles are tiring, almost no air is moving, and he is drifting off. What does that quiet chest mean?

options.text: The attack is breaking on its own
The nebulizer has finished the job
He is sliding into respiratory failure
Nebulized albuterol is making him sleepy

explanation: A fading wheeze together with exhaustion, almost no air movement, and a dropping level of alertness means he can no longer move air through tight bronchi. That is respiratory failure. Real improvement would bring louder air movement and a clearer mental status, and albuterol stimulates rather than sedates.

distractorExplanations.a: A breaking attack brings better air movement and a more alert patient. Quiet lungs plus drowsiness mean less air is moving, not recovery.
distractorExplanations.b: A nebulizer that worked would increase air movement and alertness. Silence and drifting off are fatigue, not a finished treatment.
distractorExplanations.d: Albuterol causes tremor, tachycardia, and a jittery feeling. It does not sedate, so drowsiness here is failing ventilation.

prompt: A helmeted motorcyclist lies unresponsive in the roadway with blood in the mouth, and you must open the airway before suctioning. How should you open it?

options.text: Tip the head back and lift the chin with no stabilization
Bend the neck forward until the mouth opens
Shove a pillow under the head to extend the neck
Jaw thrust while hands keep the neck still

explanation: A helmeted rider down in the roadway is treated as a cervical injury until proven otherwise. Lifting the jaw forward opens the mouth while the neck stays in line, so you can suction blood without flexion or extension.

distractorExplanations.a: Tilting the head extends the cervical spine. That is the maneuver you are trying not to use on this rider.
distractorExplanations.b: Bending the neck forward moves an unstable cervical spine and can close the airway further.
distractorExplanations.c: A pillow under the head extends or flexes the neck. It is not how you open the mouth of a downed motorcyclist.

prompt: Following a seizure, a construction worker has a strong carotid pulse but is not breathing, and the bag is attached to high-flow oxygen. How often do you deliver a breath?

options.text: About one breath every six seconds
About one breath every one to two seconds
About one breath every ten to twelve seconds
About one breath every three seconds

explanation: This worker still has a pulse and is not breathing, so adult ventilation is about one breath every 6 seconds, roughly 10 per minute, each squeeze lasting about a second and stopped when the chest rises. Faster rates raise chest pressure and cut venous return. A breath every 10 to 12 seconds under-ventilates him.

distractorExplanations.b: A breath every 1 to 2 seconds is 30 to 60 a minute. That hyperventilates an adult, stacks pressure, and drops cardiac output.
distractorExplanations.c: A breath every 10 to 12 seconds is only 5 or 6 a minute, too slow to ventilate an adult who has a pulse.
distractorExplanations.d: A breath every 3 seconds is about 20 a minute, a faster pediatric-range pace, and too quick for this adult.

prompt: Before insertion, you measure an oropharyngeal airway for an unresponsive adult who does not gag when you touch the tongue. Which landmarks give the right length?

options.text: Tip of the nose to the earlobe
Width of the patient's little finger
Center of the lips to the sternal notch
Corner of the mouth to the earlobe

explanation: Hold the airway against the cheek from the corner of the mouth to the earlobe, or to the angle of the jaw. That length lets the flange sit at the lips and the tip rest behind the tongue. Too long can fold the epiglottis down. Too short pushes the tongue backward.

distractorExplanations.a: Nose tip to earlobe is how you measure a nasopharyngeal airway, not an oropharyngeal airway.
distractorExplanations.b: Little-finger width is an old estimate for nasopharyngeal airway diameter, not for oropharyngeal length.
distractorExplanations.c: The sternal notch is not a landmark for sizing a basic airway adjunct.

prompt: Smoke exposure leaves a warehouse worker breathing 22 times a minute with good depth, a saturation of 90 percent, and no vomiting. Which oxygen device matches that pattern?

options.text: Bag-mask ventilation because breathing has stopped
A Venturi mask set to a low fixed percentage
A nonrebreather during spontaneous breathing
A nasal cannula aimed at mild hypoxia

explanation: He is breathing 22 times a minute with good depth and is hypoxic after smoke, so a reservoir mask at high flow matches a spontaneous pattern that needs a high inspired fraction. The reservoir has to stay inflated. Apnea, a low fixed percentage, and a cannula for a mild deficit describe different patients.

distractorExplanations.a: Breathing has not stopped. A bag-mask is for absent or inadequate ventilation, and this depth is adequate.
distractorExplanations.b: A low fixed Venturi percentage under-treats a saturation of 90 percent when the goal is a high inspired fraction.
distractorExplanations.d: A nasal cannula fits milder hypoxia in a stable person. Ninety percent after smoke calls for a higher fraction.

prompt: Repositioning and a two-person seal still produce no chest movement on an apneic adult, and your partner reaches for a laryngoscope and an endotracheal tube. Which airway procedure stays inside national AEMT practice?

options.text: Oral endotracheal intubation with a laryngoscope
An i-gel or other supraglottic airway
A surgical cricothyrotomy at the bedside
A needle cricothyrotomy through the neck

explanation: Bag-mask ventilation has already failed after repositioning and a two-person seal, so the next device sits above the cords and can be placed without a laryngoscope. Passing a tube through the glottis, or opening the neck with a blade or a needle, is outside national AEMT scope.

distractorExplanations.a: Oral endotracheal intubation is a paramedic skill on the national scope. Reaching for the laryngoscope does not make it an AEMT procedure.
distractorExplanations.c: Surgical cricothyrotomy is not a national AEMT airway step, even when bag-mask ventilation is failing.
distractorExplanations.d: Needle cricothyrotomy is not national AEMT scope. A supraglottic device is the advanced airway this level places.

prompt: A semiconscious warehouse clerk gags and retches the moment an oropharyngeal airway touches the tongue, though noisy respirations continue. Should that oral airway stay in his mouth?

options.text: Push it in and hold it there despite the gag
Leave the oropharyngeal airway out
Move to a surgical airway because he gagged
Cut the airway shorter and try the same route

explanation: An intact gag means this oral airway will trigger vomiting and aspiration, so it comes back out and stays out. Noisy breathing shows he is still moving air. Shortening the device or holding it against the gag does not remove that contraindication, and one gag is not a reason to open the neck.

distractorExplanations.a: Holding the airway in against a gag provokes vomiting. The gag is the contraindication, not a reflex to overpower.
distractorExplanations.c: A single gag does not create a surgical-airway indication, and surgical cricothyrotomy is outside national AEMT scope.
distractorExplanations.d: A shorter airway can still sit on the tongue and provoke vomiting. Length was not the problem. The gag was.

prompt: Clear fluid leaks from the nose of a roofer who fell, bruising sits behind one ear, and he snores. Your partner starts pushing a nasal airway upward. What should your partner do with the nasal airway?

options.text: Advance the nasal airway until resistance fades
Stop pushing the nasal airway upward
Pack the nose and leave the snoring alone
Extend the neck with a chin lift

explanation: Clear fluid from the nose plus bruising behind the ear raises concern for a basilar skull injury in this fallen roofer. A nasal airway must not be forced upward along that path. Snoring is managed by jaw position and, if he has no gag, an oral airway, without extending the neck.

distractorExplanations.a: Pushing until resistance fades is exactly the force to avoid when basilar skull findings are present.
distractorExplanations.c: Packing the nose and ignoring snoring leaves the airway obstructed and does nothing useful with the leak.
distractorExplanations.d: This is a fall. Extending the neck with a chin lift risks the cervical spine and does not address the nasal-airway hazard.

prompt: The belly swells as you bag an apneic adult with fast squeezes that empty the bag before the ribs have moved. How should the squeezes change?

options.text: Empty the whole bag as fast as possible each time
Smaller squeezes that stop when the chest rises
Aim each breath so the abdomen rises first
Speed up to about thirty breaths a minute

explanation: The swelling belly is gastric inflation from volume and speed: each squeeze is emptying the bag before the ribs move. Breaths should be slower and smaller, stopping at the first chest rise, so air goes into the lungs instead of the stomach.

distractorExplanations.a: Emptying the whole bag quickly is what is inflating the stomach. More speed and volume make the gastric distension worse.
distractorExplanations.c: A rising abdomen is the complication, not the target. Aiming there sends the breath into the esophagus.
distractorExplanations.d: Thirty breaths a minute adds more gastric inflation and raises intrathoracic pressure. The rate needs to come down, not up.

prompt: Pulmonary edema care was heading toward CPAP, but the patient is now hard to rouse, vomits, and has a systolic pressure of 78. What happens to the CPAP plan?

options.text: Apply CPAP and pull the straps tight
Do not use CPAP; suction and ventilate
A cannula now and a recheck in twenty minutes
Withhold oxygen until systolic pressure rises

explanation: CPAP needs a patient who is awake, protecting the airway, and not hypotensive. Vomiting into a tight mask, a systolic pressure of 78, and being hard to rouse are reasons to stop the plan. Clear the airway and ventilate. Oxygen itself is not withheld while you do that.

distractorExplanations.a: Tightening CPAP on a vomiting, hypotensive, hard-to-rouse patient fills the mask with vomit and can drop the pressure further.
distractorExplanations.c: A cannula and a twenty-minute wait do not clear vomit or ventilate someone who is hard to rouse.
distractorExplanations.d: Hypotension is a reason to skip CPAP, not a reason to withhold oxygen from a patient in pulmonary edema.

prompt: Pulled from a bedroom fire, a hoarse woman has soot at the nostrils and singed eyebrows, and she is still breathing. What do you do while air is still moving?

options.text: Transport now on oxygen, ready to assist
Remain on scene until the hoarseness clears
Stay to pick a more comfortable oxygen mask
Skip oxygen because the facial burn looks minor

explanation: Hoarseness, nasal soot, and singed eyebrows after an enclosed fire mean the airway can swell shut. Oxygen starts and transport starts, with a plan to assist ventilation if the swelling progresses. Waiting for the voice to clear, or lingering over a more comfortable mask, uses minutes the swelling may not give you.

distractorExplanations.b: Hoarseness after a bedroom fire is a reason to leave, not a finding to watch until it fades. Swelling can close the airway while you wait there.
distractorExplanations.c: Debating a more comfortable mask on scene delays transport. The mask is not the time-critical decision. The swelling airway is.
distractorExplanations.d: A face that looks only mildly reddened does not cancel soot, singed brows, and a hoarse voice. She still needs oxygen.

prompt: At a diner, a conscious patron clutches the throat, cannot speak or cough, and turns dusky while a coworker lines up a blind finger sweep. What replaces the finger sweep?

options.text: Give abdominal thrusts from behind him
Allow a blind finger sweep while he is awake
Give five back blows plus five chest thrusts
Coach him to cough the object out himself

explanation: A conscious adult who cannot speak or cough has a complete obstruction. Abdominal thrusts are the maneuver, and a finger goes in the mouth only if you can see the object. He cannot cough it out, and the infant back-blow sequence is the wrong age.

distractorExplanations.b: A blind finger sweep in an awake choking adult can push the object deeper. Sweep only when the object is visible.
distractorExplanations.c: Five back blows and five chest thrusts are the infant sequence. This dusky patron is a conscious adult.
distractorExplanations.d: Coaching a cough fits a partial obstruction with an effective cough. He cannot speak or cough, so that window is already closed.

prompt: An awake eight-month-old in a high chair suddenly cannot cry or cough, makes no sound, and turns gray during a feeding, while a relative begins abdominal thrusts. What sequence should replace those thrusts?

options.text: Five back blows, then five chest thrusts
Repeated abdominal thrusts above the navel
A blind finger sweep across the tongue
Watching and waiting until a cry returns

explanation: This awake infant is silent and gray with a sudden obstruction during feeding, so the sequence is five back blows alternating with five chest thrusts, repeated until the object moves or the infant becomes unresponsive. Abdominal thrusts risk organ injury at this age.

distractorExplanations.b: Abdominal thrusts are for a conscious adult or child, not an eight-month-old. They can injure the abdomen and are the maneuver the relative should stop.
distractorExplanations.c: A blind finger sweep can push the object farther down. Nothing in the mouth was seen.
distractorExplanations.d: A silent, gray infant is not a watch-and-wait problem. Air is not moving, and the obstruction will not clear by observation.

prompt: A total laryngectomy left a neck stoma with no tube in it, breathing is inadequate, and your partner seals a mask over the mouth and nose. Where does the bag-mask seal belong?

options.text: Leave the mask sealed on the mouth and nose
Cover the stoma and bag through the mouth
Seal the bag-mask on the neck stoma
Intubate through the mouth and ignore the stoma

explanation: After a total laryngectomy the trachea opens on the neck and no longer connects to the mouth or nose. Inadequate breathing is ventilated by sealing the bag-mask on that stoma. Air pushed into the mouth never reaches the lungs, and covering the stoma blocks the only route.

distractorExplanations.a: Sealing the mouth and nose leaves the lungs unventilated, because that route was disconnected at the laryngectomy.
distractorExplanations.b: Covering the stoma and bagging the mouth occludes the only opening to the lungs and sends the breath into a blind upper tract.
distractorExplanations.d: An oral tube does not reach the trachea after a total laryngectomy, and oral intubation is outside national AEMT scope anyway.

prompt: Adult cardiac arrest care has just reached a supraglottic airway in place, with a confirming carbon-dioxide waveform, while compressions still pause every thirty counts. How should compressions and breaths run from here?

options.text: Keep pausing compressions every thirty counts for two breaths
Stop compressions and squeeze the bag alone
Compress without pauses and give a breath every 6 seconds
Give a breath every 2 seconds and pause each time

explanation: Once the supraglottic airway is in place and the waveform confirms it, adult arrest ventilation no longer waits for a pause. Compressions continue, and one breath is given every 6 seconds. The 30:2 pause was for bag-mask ventilation before that airway was in place.

distractorExplanations.a: Pausing every 30 compressions for two breaths is the ratio used before an advanced airway. That pause stops once the supraglottic airway is in and confirmed.
distractorExplanations.b: Stopping compressions to bag removes coronary perfusion. The airway change does not replace chest compressions.
distractorExplanations.d: A breath every 2 seconds is far too fast during adult arrest and, with a pause each time, brings back the interruption you just left.

prompt: Bagged breaths continue, and a finger probe has drifted from 90 to 93 percent, but you still cannot tell whether each squeeze reaches the lungs. Which reading shows that each squeeze is ventilating?

options.text: The pulse oximeter number on its own
A return of pink color in the lips
Waveform capnography on each breath
How soft or hard the bag feels

explanation: A waveform that rises and falls with each squeeze shows exhaled carbon dioxide, which means air reached the lungs and came back. The oximeter on this patient has only drifted from 90 to 93, and that number lags and can move for reasons other than the breath just delivered. Lip color and bag feel do not measure ventilation.

distractorExplanations.a: The climb from 90 to 93 lags the breath and can reflect circulation or earlier oxygen, so the oximeter alone does not prove this squeeze ventilated.
distractorExplanations.b: Pink lips are a late, crude color change. They do not show whether the breath you just gave reached the alveoli.
distractorExplanations.d: Bag feel reflects seal, compliance, and resistance. A soft bag can still be leaking, and a firm bag can still be ventilating poorly.

prompt: Known chronic lung disease accompanies a hypoxic man at 86 percent who speaks in broken phrases, and your partner wants oxygen withheld so the drive to breathe stays intact. What do you do about his oxygen?

options.text: Withhold oxygen to protect the hypoxic drive
Pass an endotracheal tube before any oxygen
Give oxygen and keep checking ventilation
Open the neck with a surgical airway first

explanation: A saturation of 86 percent is treated with oxygen even when the history is chronic lung disease. The fear of removing a hypoxic drive is not a reason to leave this man hypoxic while he is still speaking. Ventilation is watched as oxygen is given. A tube or a surgical airway is not the first national AEMT move.

distractorExplanations.a: Withholding oxygen to protect a hypoxic drive leaves dangerous hypoxemia in place. Hypoxia is treated, and breathing is monitored.
distractorExplanations.b: He is speaking in broken phrases, so he is breathing. Oral intubation is outside national AEMT scope and is not a prerequisite for oxygen.
distractorExplanations.d: A surgical airway is not indicated by chronic lung disease plus hypoxia, and it is outside national AEMT scope.

prompt: Sized and ready, an oropharyngeal airway is about to go into an unresponsive adult without a gag, but a new partner aims the tip straight at the top of the head. How should you insert it?

options.text: Shove the tip straight toward the top of the head
Seat it no deeper than the front teeth
Twirl it several times and leave it sideways
Curve it along the palate or rotate it in

explanation: In this adult the oral airway follows the curve of the palate, using a tongue blade if needed, or it is inserted and rotated into position so the tip ends behind the tongue. Driving it straight at the skull, stopping at the teeth, or parking it sideways leaves the tongue in the way.

distractorExplanations.a: Aiming the tip at the top of the head and shoving drives it into the palate or the tongue instead of seating it behind the tongue.
distractorExplanations.b: Stopping at the front teeth leaves the tongue against the posterior pharynx, so the oral airway never does its job.
distractorExplanations.c: Spinning it and leaving it sideways does not follow the pharyngeal curve and does not hold the tongue forward.

prompt: Two minutes of assisted breaths later, the man who had been apneic now breathes at a normal depth, opens his eyes, and follows simple commands. Do you keep squeezing the bag?

options.text: Continue bagging at the same rate and volume
Roll him over and give no supplemental oxygen
Start CPAP now that his eyes are open
Stop bagging, apply oxygen, and reassess

explanation: Normal depth, open eyes, and the ability to follow commands mean his own ventilation has returned, so forced bag breaths stop. Those extra breaths would inflate the stomach and fight his drive. He still gets oxygen, and rate, depth, and saturation are checked again rather than assumed solved.

distractorExplanations.a: Continuing the same bag rate on a person who is breathing and following commands causes gastric inflation and works against his own respiratory drive.
distractorExplanations.b: Adequate breathing is a reason to stop the bag, not a reason to remove oxygen. He still needs supplemental oxygen and a fresh set of vitals.
distractorExplanations.c: Open eyes do not create a CPAP indication. CPAP is for selected awake patients in pulmonary edema or COPD distress, which this recovery does not describe.

prompt: A preschooler still has a pulse but moves almost no air after a febrile seizure, and your partner copies an adult cadence. Which pace replaces that adult cadence?

options.text: Six breaths each minute, one every ten seconds
Ten breaths each minute, one every six seconds
Fifteen breaths each minute, one every four seconds
Twenty to thirty breaths each minute

explanation: A child with a pulse and inadequate breathing is ventilated about once every 2 to 3 seconds, which is 20 to 30 breaths a minute. The adult pace of one breath every 6 seconds, and the slower rates beside it, do not move enough air for this preschooler. No drug dose replaces those breaths.

distractorExplanations.a: Six breaths a minute is too slow for any age here and would leave this preschooler hypoventilated.
distractorExplanations.b: Ten breaths a minute, one every 6 seconds, is the adult-with-a-pulse pace your partner copied. It is too slow for a child.
distractorExplanations.c: Fifteen breaths a minute is still slower than the pediatric rescue rate of about one breath every 2 to 3 seconds.

prompt: A 46-year-old warehouse worker is sweaty and confused, and the meter reads 48 mg/dL. He drinks a sip of water without coughing and follows a simple command. Which hypoglycemia treatment fits this AEMT situation?

options.text: Insulin injection by EMT basic without protocol
Large IV potassium bolus
Withholding all sugar indefinitely
Oral glucose per protocol

explanation: He is symptomatic and hypoglycemic, but he can swallow and protect his airway, so oral glucose is the protocol treatment. Insulin would drive the glucose lower. A potassium bolus is not a field hypoglycemia drug, and withholding sugar leaves the brain without fuel.

distractorExplanations.a: Insulin lowers blood glucose. Giving it to a patient who is already at 48 mg/dL deepens the hypoglycemia.
distractorExplanations.b: A potassium bolus is not a treatment for low blood sugar, and a rapid IV potassium dose is dangerous.
distractorExplanations.c: Withholding sugar leaves a symptomatic hypoglycemic patient without the fuel his brain is missing.

prompt: A 28-year-old woman was stung by a bee. She is wheezing, her tongue is swelling, and her systolic pressure has fallen to 78 mm Hg. Which medication is the treatment priority?

options.text: Intramuscular epinephrine
Oral antihistamine only as sole therapy
Aspirin tablets by mouth
Nitroglycerin

explanation: Two systems are failing at once: the airway is swelling and wheezing, and the pressure has crashed. Intramuscular epinephrine is the priority drug in anaphylaxis. An antihistamine, aspirin, or nitroglycerin does not restore pressure or open this airway.

distractorExplanations.b: An oral antihistamine may ease itching later. It is not the drug that treats airway swelling and shock, and it is not given as the only therapy.
distractorExplanations.c: Aspirin is an antiplatelet drug for suspected coronary syndrome. It does not treat anaphylaxis.
distractorExplanations.d: Nitroglycerin drops blood pressure further. This patient is already hypotensive from anaphylaxis.

prompt: A 60-year-old man has pressure-like chest pain that spreads into his jaw, and the protocol calls for aspirin. What is the main early reason that aspirin is given in suspected acute coronary syndrome?

options.text: Dissolves established fibrin clots like fibrinolytics in the field
Inhibits platelet aggregation and may reduce clot progression
Dilates coronary arteries to relieve the chest pain quickly
Relieves cardiac pain as an analgesic at this low dose

explanation: Early aspirin helps because it inhibits platelet aggregation, which can slow growth of the clot in a coronary artery. It does not dissolve a fibrin clot the way a hospital fibrinolytic might, it does not open the artery by dilation, and this dose is not being given as a painkiller.

distractorExplanations.a: Fibrinolytics break down established fibrin clots and are a hospital decision. Aspirin does not do that work in the field.
distractorExplanations.c: Coronary dilation is the story told about nitroglycerin, not about aspirin. Aspirin acts on platelets.
distractorExplanations.d: The chewed aspirin dose used for chest pain is an antiplatelet dose, not an analgesic dose aimed at the pain itself.

prompt: A 19-year-old runner is speaking in short phrases, with wheezes in every lung field, after practice in cold air. You give an inhaled albuterol treatment. How does that drug ease the attack?

options.text: Blocking beta-2 receptors so the bronchial smooth muscle relaxes
Stimulating beta-2 receptors to relax bronchial smooth muscle
Reducing airway inflammation over the next several hours
Thinning mucus so it can be coughed up more easily

explanation: Albuterol stimulates beta-2 receptors, and that stimulation relaxes bronchial smooth muscle so air can move. Blocking those receptors would tighten the airways. Albuterol is not the drug that treats inflammation over hours, and it is not a mucus-thinning agent.

distractorExplanations.a: Blocking beta-2 receptors would oppose bronchodilation. Albuterol stimulates those receptors.
distractorExplanations.c: Swelling and inflammation are a slower process, often treated later with steroids. The immediate relief from albuterol is smooth-muscle relaxation.
distractorExplanations.d: Mucus thinning is a different drug effect. Albuterol's main action in an acute attack is opening constricted bronchi.

prompt: An adult was stabbed in the flank. The skin is pale and cool, he is confused, the radial pulse is weak, and you cannot find external bleeding to stop. How is isotonic IV fluid usually titrated in this hemorrhagic shock?

options.text: Restore a normal systolic pressure of about 120 mmHg
Run wide open until the patient's lungs sound wet
Give exactly 3 liters before any reassessment
Minimal perfusion, such as a radial pulse

explanation: Uncontrolled internal bleeding does not get a chase to a normal blood pressure. Isotonic fluid is titrated to a sign of minimal perfusion, such as a returning radial pulse, then reassessed. Flooding until the lungs are wet, or dumping a fixed 3 liters, can wash out clot and worsen the bleed.

distractorExplanations.a: Pushing the systolic pressure back to about 120 mm Hg before bleeding is controlled can disrupt clot and increase hemorrhage.
distractorExplanations.b: Running fluid until the lungs sound wet is fluid overload, not a resuscitation target.
distractorExplanations.c: A fixed 3-liter volume without reassessment ignores whether perfusion has already returned.

prompt: You are about to give a protocol medication to an adult with chest pain who is awake and matches the vial in your hand. Which set of checks is the core rights of administration before that drug is given?

options.text: Right diagnosis, protocol, medical director, and destination
Right patient, drug, dose, route, and time, then document
Right vehicle, crew, radio channel, and destination
Right expiration date, lot number, packaging, and storage

explanation: Before the drug leaves your hand you confirm the right patient, the right drug, the right dose, the right route, and the right time, and you document it. Expiration, lot number, and allergies are extra safety checks. The ambulance destination and the radio channel are not medication rights.

distractorExplanations.a: The protocol and the medical director authorize a drug class. They are not the five checks made on this patient at the moment of administration.
distractorExplanations.c: Vehicle, crew, radio channel, and destination are operational details. They do not confirm the medication about to be given.
distractorExplanations.d: Expiration and clarity matter, but lot number, packaging, and storage are not the core rights of patient, drug, dose, route, and time.

prompt: A critically ill adult in shock has had two failed attempts at a peripheral IV, and the protocol allows a deeper vascular route. Which access gives the fastest reliable path for fluids and medications?

options.text: Intramuscular injection into the deltoid
Subcutaneous infusion in the abdomen
Sublingual placement of oral medications
Intraosseous (IO) access

explanation: When a peripheral vein cannot be cannulated in a critically ill adult, intraosseous access reaches the vascular space through the bone marrow and can be placed quickly. A deltoid injection, a subcutaneous drip, or a pill under the tongue is not a reliable route for resuscitation fluids in this patient.

distractorExplanations.a: An intramuscular injection does not provide the vascular access this patient needs for fluids and emergency medications.
distractorExplanations.b: Subcutaneous fluid is slow and unreliable in shock, when skin perfusion is poor.
distractorExplanations.c: A sublingual tablet is not vascular access, and an unresponsive or shocked patient may not be able to take anything by mouth.

prompt: Epinephrine has just been given to an adult in anaphylaxis. The blood pressure starts to climb and the facial swelling eases, while the wheeze is a separate problem. Which epinephrine effect mainly explains that vascular change?

options.text: Relaxing bronchial smooth muscle to relieve wheezing
Constricting vessels to raise pressure and cut swelling
Slowing the heart rate so the ventricles fill better
Blocking histamine receptors to stop the hives and itching

explanation: Alpha-1 stimulation constricts blood vessels. That raises the pressure and reduces the mucosal edema. Relaxing bronchial muscle is the beta-2 effect, a faster heart rate is beta-1, and epinephrine does not block histamine receptors the way an antihistamine does.

distractorExplanations.a: Bronchial relaxation is a beta-2 effect and can ease wheezing. It is not the effect that raises pressure and shrinks swelling.
distractorExplanations.c: Epinephrine does not slow the heart to improve filling. Beta-1 stimulation tends to increase rate and contractility.
distractorExplanations.d: Histamine-receptor blockade is what an antihistamine does. Epinephrine's pressure effect here is vasoconstriction.

prompt: An adult with suspected cardiac chest pain has a systolic pressure of 128 mm Hg and has not taken a PDE-5 inhibitor. What is the usual sublingual nitroglycerin dose and repeat interval in a typical AEMT protocol?

options.text: 0.04 mg sublingual, repeated every minute
0.4 mg sublingual, repeated every 15 minutes
0.4 mg sublingual, repeated every 5 minutes
40 mg intramuscular in the deltoid

explanation: The usual adult dose is 0.4 mg under the tongue, repeated about every 5 minutes while the pain continues and the blood pressure stays adequate, often up to three doses. A 0.04 mg dose is a decimal-place error, every 15 minutes is too slow for this protocol, and 40 mg in the muscle is not nitroglycerin dosing.

distractorExplanations.a: 0.04 mg is ten times too small, and repeating it every minute is not the protocol interval.
distractorExplanations.b: 0.4 mg is the right tablet size, but every 15 minutes is not the usual repeat interval while pain and pressure allow another dose.
distractorExplanations.d: 40 mg intramuscularly is not a nitroglycerin dose or route for suspected cardiac chest pain.

prompt: An adult with suspected acute coronary syndrome has no aspirin allergy and is not actively bleeding. He can chew and swallow. How is the aspirin usually given?

options.text: 1 g dissolved under the tongue every hour
81 mg swallowed whole with a full glass of water
650 mg given slowly through an IV line
160–325 mg chewed (often four 81 mg tablets)

explanation: Chewing 162 to 325 mg, commonly four 81 mg tablets for 324 mg, speeds absorption and platelet inhibition. Swallowing a single 81 mg tablet is a daily-prevention dose, not the early coronary dose. Aspirin is not given as 1 g under the tongue or as 650 mg through an IV.

distractorExplanations.a: One gram under the tongue every hour is not the aspirin regimen for suspected coronary syndrome.
distractorExplanations.b: A single 81 mg tablet swallowed whole is the low daily dose. The early coronary dose is chewed and is several of those tablets.
distractorExplanations.c: Aspirin for this indication is chewed, not pushed slowly through an IV at 650 mg.

prompt: A man is unresponsive with slow breathing after injecting heroin. Ventilation is underway, naloxone is given, and his breathing improves. Why does naloxone reverse an opioid overdose?

options.text: Blocks opioid receptors and displaces the opioid
Stimulates beta-2 receptors to open the airways
Reverses benzodiazepines at the GABA receptor
Raises blood glucose by releasing liver glycogen

explanation: Naloxone is a competitive antagonist at opioid receptors. It displaces the opioid and can restore breathing. It does not open airways through beta-2 receptors, it does not reverse benzodiazepines, and it does not raise glucose by releasing liver glycogen.

distractorExplanations.b: Beta-2 stimulation is how albuterol relaxes bronchial muscle. Naloxone does not work that way.
distractorExplanations.c: Benzodiazepines act at the GABA receptor. Naloxone does not reverse them.
distractorExplanations.d: Releasing liver glycogen is glucagon's mechanism. Naloxone does not treat hypoglycemia.

prompt: An adult has cardiac-sounding chest pain and otherwise looks like a nitroglycerin candidate. Which finding makes sublingual nitroglycerin the wrong drug right now?

options.text: Recent PDE-5 inhibitor use or hypotension
Chest pain lasting more than 5 minutes
A systolic blood pressure of 110 mm Hg or higher
The patient already took aspirin today

explanation: Nitroglycerin dilates vessels and can drop the blood pressure hard. Recent use of a PDE-5 inhibitor, or a pressure that is already low, is a contraindication. Pain that has lasted more than five minutes is a reason to treat, not a reason to withhold it. Aspirin and nitroglycerin are used together when both are allowed.

distractorExplanations.b: Pain lasting more than five minutes is consistent with ischemia. Duration alone does not contraindicate nitroglycerin.
distractorExplanations.c: A systolic pressure of 110 mm Hg or higher is in the range where a protocol often still allows nitroglycerin, not a reason to withhold it.
distractorExplanations.d: Aspirin does not block nitroglycerin. The two drugs answer different parts of suspected coronary syndrome.

prompt: An adult in anaphylaxis is wheezing, with a systolic pressure of 84 mm Hg. You are drawing up epinephrine. How is the intramuscular dose typically given?

options.text: 1 mg of the 0.1 mg/mL concentration as a rapid IV push
0.3–0.5 mg of the 1 mg/mL concentration into the lateral thigh
3–5 mg of the 1 mg/mL concentration under the tongue
0.03 mg of the 0.1 mg/mL concentration into the deltoid muscle

explanation: Adult intramuscular epinephrine for anaphylaxis is 0.3 to 0.5 mg of the 1 mg/mL concentration, injected into the mid-anterolateral thigh. One milligram of the dilute 0.1 mg/mL concentration as a rapid IV push is the cardiac-arrest concentration and dose, not this injection. Under the tongue, or a hundred-fold smaller dose in the deltoid, is not the protocol.

distractorExplanations.a: 1 mg of 0.1 mg/mL given as a rapid IV push is cardiac-arrest epinephrine. That dose and route are not the anaphylaxis injection.
distractorExplanations.c: Several milligrams under the tongue is not how intramuscular anaphylaxis epinephrine is given.
distractorExplanations.d: 0.03 mg of the dilute concentration in the deltoid is far too small and is the wrong site and concentration.

prompt: An unresponsive adult has a blood glucose of 38 mg/dL, no gag reflex, and a patent IV already running in the forearm. What is the preferred treatment in a typical AEMT protocol?

options.text: Oral glucose paste placed between cheek and gum
IM glucagon first, saving IV dextrose for a failed response
IV dextrose (for example D10 or D50) per protocol
Oxygen only, then recheck glucose in 15 minutes

explanation: He cannot swallow, so paste in the cheek is an aspiration risk. The IV is already in, so dextrose through that line, D10 or D50 as the protocol specifies, is the fastest correction. Glucagon is the fallback when a line cannot be obtained. Oxygen alone does not raise a glucose of 38 mg/dL.

distractorExplanations.a: Oral paste in an unresponsive patient with no gag reflex can be aspirated. The line is already available.
distractorExplanations.b: Glucagon is for the patient you cannot get a line on. Here the IV is patent, so dextrose comes first.
distractorExplanations.d: Oxygen does not correct hypoglycemia. Waiting 15 minutes to recheck leaves the glucose at 38 mg/dL.

prompt: A confused adult has a blood glucose of 42 mg/dL, cannot swallow safely, and two IV attempts have failed. When is glucagon the most useful hypoglycemia treatment?

options.text: The patient has no liver glycogen stores at all
The patient is alert and able to drink juice safely
IV dextrose is available and a line is already running
IV access cannot be obtained

explanation: Glucagon, given intramuscularly or intranasally, tells the liver to release stored glycogen. It is the fallback when IV dextrose cannot be given and the patient cannot take oral glucose. It works poorly if the liver has no glycogen stores. It is not the first choice in an alert patient who can drink, or when a dextrose line is already running.

distractorExplanations.a: Without liver glycogen, glucagon has little glucose to release. Chronic malnutrition is a reason it may fail, not the situation where it is most useful.
distractorExplanations.b: An alert patient who can drink juice should get oral sugar. Glucagon is not required.
distractorExplanations.c: If IV dextrose is running, that is the direct treatment. Glucagon is not preferred over a working line.

prompt: A 54-year-old man is unresponsive after his morning insulin. The meter reads 36 mg/dL, and he does not gag when you suction. His partner holds a tube of oral glucose paste. Where should that paste go?

options.text: Nowhere in the mouth, because he cannot protect the airway
Between the cheek and the gum so it can absorb there
On the tongue so the next breath carries it down
Mixed into water and poured slowly past the teeth

explanation: An unresponsive patient who does not gag cannot protect the airway. Glucose paste in the mouth is an aspiration risk. This is a different patient from the awake person who can swallow. The sugar has to arrive by vein, or by glucagon if a vein cannot be found.

distractorExplanations.b: Cheek-and-gum placement is for a patient who can protect the airway. This man does not gag.
distractorExplanations.c: Putting paste on the tongue of an unresponsive patient sends it toward the lungs, not the blood.
distractorExplanations.d: Pouring liquid into an unprotected airway is aspiration. He needs a route that is not the mouth.

prompt: A 40-year-old woman has hives, wheezing, and a blood pressure of 82/50 after eating shrimp. Two epinephrine concentrations are in the kit. Which administration matches adult anaphylaxis?

options.text: 0.3 mg of the 1 mg/mL concentration, intramuscular, mid-thigh
1 mg of the 0.1 mg/mL concentration as a rapid intravenous push
0.3 mg of the 1 mg/mL concentration placed under the tongue
3 mg of the 1 mg/mL concentration injected into the deltoid

explanation: Adult anaphylaxis epinephrine is 0.3 mg of the 1 mg/mL concentration, injected into the mid-anterolateral thigh. The 0.1 mg/mL vial given as 1 mg by rapid IV push is the cardiac-arrest concentration and dose. Under the tongue, or 3 mg in the deltoid, is not this protocol.

distractorExplanations.b: That is cardiac-arrest epinephrine: a tenfold concentration error and the wrong route for anaphylaxis.
distractorExplanations.c: The 0.3 mg dose is right only as an intramuscular thigh injection, not under the tongue.
distractorExplanations.d: Three milligrams in the deltoid is many times the anaphylaxis dose and the wrong muscle.

prompt: A 70-year-old man suddenly cannot lift his right arm, and his words are slurred. He coughs and chokes when you offer a sip of water. What is the aspirin decision on this call?

options.text: Do not give aspirin; move him to a stroke-capable hospital
Give 324 mg chewed, the same early dose used for chest pain
Give one 81 mg tablet swallowed whole once the cough stops
Give aspirin only after the glucometer also reads low

explanation: This is a stroke-like emergency, and he cannot swallow safely. Aspirin is an acute-coronary drug, not the field treatment for stroke, and a sip that makes him choke is a reason not to put anything in the mouth. The priority is recognition, glucose only as a check you can do without oral medicine, and rapid transport.

distractorExplanations.b: The chewed 324 mg dose belongs to suspected coronary syndrome. It is not the field treatment for a stroke, and he is choking on water.
distractorExplanations.c: Waiting to swallow an 81 mg tablet delays transport and still puts a pill in a patient who cannot protect his airway.
distractorExplanations.d: A low glucose can mimic a stroke and would be treated as hypoglycemia. Aspirin is not the treatment for either problem.

prompt: A 66-year-old woman has heavy chest pressure, pale cold skin, and a blood pressure of 78/50. She has no aspirin allergy and has not taken aspirin today. Which medication plan fits?

options.text: Aspirin if it is safe to swallow, and no nitroglycerin
Nitroglycerin 0.4 mg now, and aspirin once you are driving
Neither drug, because the low pressure will limit the clot
Nitroglycerin every five minutes until the pressure recovers

explanation: She looks like an acute coronary syndrome patient who is already in shock. Nitroglycerin dilates vessels and can drop this pressure further, so it is withheld. Aspirin still inhibits platelets if she can swallow it safely and has no bleeding contraindication. Skipping both drugs because the pressure is low leaves the platelet problem untreated.

distractorExplanations.b: Leading with nitroglycerin at 78 mm Hg systolic can worsen shock. Aspirin is the drug that still fits.
distractorExplanations.c: Hypotension is a reason to hold nitroglycerin. It is not a reason to skip aspirin when she can take it.
distractorExplanations.d: Repeating nitroglycerin until the pressure rises reverses the physiology. Nitroglycerin lowers pressure.

prompt: A 58-year-old man with cardiac-sounding pain has already taken three 0.4 mg nitroglycerin tablets. His blood pressure is 118/74 and the pain has not changed. What is the next medication step?

options.text: Stop at three nitroglycerin doses and transport him
Give a fourth 0.4 mg tablet because the pressure still allows it
Switch to 40 mg of nitroglycerin injected in the deltoid
Repeat 0.4 mg every minute until the chest pain breaks

explanation: Typical protocols cap nitroglycerin at three doses of 0.4 mg about five minutes apart, then stop even if the pain remains and the pressure is still adequate. A fourth tablet, a 40 mg injection, or a dose every minute is outside that limit. Aspirin, a 12-lead if you can send one, and transport are the next actions, not more nitroglycerin.

distractorExplanations.b: An adequate blood pressure lets you give the doses the protocol allows. It does not authorize a fourth dose past the usual maximum.
distractorExplanations.c: Forty milligrams in the deltoid is not a nitroglycerin dose or route.
distractorExplanations.d: Every minute is far more frequent than the 3-to-5-minute interval, and three doses are already in.

prompt: A 72-year-old man sits bolt upright, gasping, with crackles in both lungs and a blood pressure of 86/60 after an hour of chest pressure. Your partner opens a liter of saline and wants it wide open. What is the better fluid decision?

options.text: Run the liter wide open until the systolic pressure reaches 120
Give that bolus, then add sublingual nitroglycerin for the pressure
Do not flood wet lungs; support breathing and transport
Withhold every treatment until a chest film is done on scene

explanation: Crackles, upright posture, and hypotension after chest pain point to pump failure, not to a dry patient who needs a large saline bolus. A wide-open liter can push more fluid into the alveoli. Nitroglycerin on top of a pressure of 86 mm Hg is also the wrong add-on. Breathing support and transport matter more than filling the vascular space.

distractorExplanations.a: Chasing a normal systolic number with a wide-open bolus treats hypovolemia. These lungs are already wet.
distractorExplanations.b: Nitroglycerin at 86 mm Hg systolic can drop the pressure further. It does not rescue a bad fluid bolus.
distractorExplanations.d: Waiting on scene for an x-ray delays care he cannot get in the ambulance bay of a living room.

prompt: A 63-year-old woman with heart failure is coughing pink froth. You hear crackles and no wheeze. Her son asks you to start the neighbor's albuterol because she looks short of breath. What does inhaled albuterol actually treat?

options.text: Fluid that has leaked into the alveoli of pulmonary edema
A clot sitting inside a coronary artery during ischemia
Bronchospasm from tightened bronchial smooth muscle
A falling blood sugar that is making her breathe hard

explanation: Albuterol relaxes bronchial smooth muscle. It is the drug for bronchospasm, which you would hear as wheeze. Pink froth and crackles are fluid in the alveoli, and albuterol does not push that fluid out. It also does not inhibit platelets or raise glucose.

distractorExplanations.a: Pulmonary edema is fluid, not bronchospasm. A bronchodilator does not clear the alveoli.
distractorExplanations.b: Platelet inhibition in ischemia is aspirin's job. Albuterol does not treat a coronary clot.
distractorExplanations.d: Albuterol is not a treatment for hypoglycemia, and this story is not a low-glucose story.

prompt: A man has hives, wheezing, and a falling blood pressure after a new antibiotic. The only nebulizer vial a partner grabs is ipratropium, and he wants that to be the only drug. What is ipratropium's actual job?

options.text: It replaces epinephrine as the priority drug in anaphylaxis
It constricts vessels the way epinephrine's alpha-1 effect does
It is an add-on bronchodilator, not the anaphylaxis drug
It reverses the allergen by blocking opioid receptors

explanation: Ipratropium is an anticholinergic bronchodilator used as an adjunct in bronchospasm. Anaphylaxis with low pressure and hives needs intramuscular epinephrine first. Ipratropium does not constrict vessels, and it is not an opioid antagonist.

distractorExplanations.a: Nothing in the nebulizer cup replaces epinephrine when pressure is falling and hives are present.
distractorExplanations.b: Vasoconstriction in anaphylaxis is epinephrine's alpha-1 effect. Ipratropium does not do that.
distractorExplanations.d: Opioid-receptor blockade is naloxone. Ipratropium does not reverse an allergen that way.

prompt: A 17-year-old is hard to rouse after taking several alprazolam tablets and nothing else. Breathing is slow, and there is no opioid history. A classmate says naloxone will reverse those pills. What is true of naloxone here?

options.text: It reverses benzodiazepines at the GABA receptor
It is the same antidote used for a beta-blocker overdose
It blocks opioid receptors and will not reverse alprazolam
It raises glucose by releasing glycogen from the liver

explanation: Naloxone competes at opioid receptors only. Alprazolam is a benzodiazepine and acts at GABA, so naloxone does not reverse it. Ventilation is the treatment while you transport. Naloxone is also not a beta-blocker antidote and does not release liver glycogen.

distractorExplanations.a: Benzodiazepines are not opioids. Naloxone has no reversing effect at the GABA receptor.
distractorExplanations.b: A beta blocker is a different overdose. Naloxone is not its antidote.
distractorExplanations.d: Glycogen release is glucagon. Naloxone does not correct a glucose problem, and this call is not hypoglycemia.

prompt: You are about to draw a protocol drug and notice the vial in your hand is a different strength than the card, and the expiration stamp is last month. What fails if you give it anyway?

options.text: Only the paperwork, which the hospital can finish later
Nothing important, because the patient already consented
The right drug strength and a supply that is still in date
The driving route chosen to reach the receiving hospital

explanation: A different concentration is the wrong dose waiting to happen, and an expired vial is not a usable supply. Consent to care does not authorize the wrong strength. The hospital's later charting does not fix a drug error made now, and the driving route has nothing to do with the vial.

distractorExplanations.a: Documentation records what you gave. It does not make an expired, wrong-strength vial into the right drug.
distractorExplanations.b: Consent covers treatment. It does not cover giving a concentration the protocol did not name.
distractorExplanations.d: The route to the hospital is an operations choice. It is not the medication check that just failed.

prompt: A wheezing woman has her own prescribed albuterol inhaler in her purse. A bystander offers a handful of unidentified white tablets and says they are for breathing. What may you assist under a typical protocol?

options.text: The loose tablets, because the bystander vouched for them
Both the tablets and the inhaler, to cover every receptor
Her own prescribed inhaler, not a stranger's loose pills
Neither one, because this level cannot touch any inhaler

explanation: Assisting with the patient's own prescribed inhaler is a standard protocol action when the drug and the patient match. Unidentified tablets from a bystander fail the right-drug check. Giving both adds an unknown drug. Refusing the prescribed inhaler withholds a drug the protocol allows.

distractorExplanations.a: A bystander's word does not identify a tablet. Unknown pills are not a protocol medication.
distractorExplanations.b: Adding an unidentified tablet to a known inhaler does not make the tablet safer.
distractorExplanations.d: Helping with the patient's own prescribed bronchodilator inhaler is within a typical AEMT protocol.

prompt: The written protocol lists a fixed epinephrine dose for anaphylaxis. The family asks you to double it because the patient is a large adult, and medical control has not approved a change. What should you do?

options.text: Double it, because body size always overrides the written card
Give the written dose, or call medical control before any change
Skip epinephrine until a pharmacist calculates a new amount
Use the cardiac-arrest intravenous dose so the size is covered

explanation: The protocol is the authorization. A family request to double a dose is not a protocol change. If the situation truly sits outside the card, you call medical control before you invent a new amount. Skipping epinephrine in anaphylaxis, or substituting the cardiac-arrest IV dose, is the more dangerous move.

distractorExplanations.a: Body size does not silently rewrite a fixed protocol dose. A change needs medical control.
distractorExplanations.c: Waiting for a pharmacist withholds the drug anaphylaxis needs now. The written dose is already authorized.
distractorExplanations.d: The intravenous cardiac-arrest dose is a different concentration and a different indication.

prompt: An adult with crushing chest pain is vomiting over and over and cannot keep saliva in his mouth. The protocol lists chewed aspirin, and he has no allergy. What is the safe decision about that oral dose?

options.text: Crush it and place it on the back of the tongue anyway
Do not give an oral drug while he cannot protect the airway
Push 650 mg of aspirin slowly through the intravenous line
Replace the aspirin with a nitroglycerin tablet for the vomiting

explanation: Chewed aspirin only helps if it stays in the stomach and he can protect his airway. Repeated vomiting with secretions he cannot manage is a reason to hold the oral dose, not to force it to the back of the tongue. Aspirin is not an IV push in this protocol, and nitroglycerin does not become the substitute just because he is vomiting.

distractorExplanations.a: Forcing a crushed tablet into the throat of a vomiting patient is an aspiration, not a faster dose.
distractorExplanations.c: The coronary aspirin dose is chewed. It is not 650 mg given slowly by vein.
distractorExplanations.d: Vomiting is not an indication to swap aspirin for nitroglycerin. Each drug has its own contraindications.

prompt: You gave intravenous dextrose to an unresponsive adult whose glucose was 34 mg/dL. He is opening his eyes and mumbling. What still has to happen before you treat the problem as finished?

options.text: Clear the call on scene, since one dose means he is cured
Give insulin next so the glucose cannot climb too high
Tuck oral glucose in the cheek while he is still groggy
Recheck the glucose and keep watching his mental status

explanation: Dextrose can wear off, especially if long-acting insulin is still on board. Opening his eyes is a response, not a finished call. You recheck the number and watch whether he stays awake. Insulin is not an AEMT follow-up, and paste in the cheek of a still-groggy patient risks aspiration.

distractorExplanations.a: One dose can rebound downward. Leaving him on scene because he mumbled once skips the reassessment.
distractorExplanations.b: Insulin would drop the glucose you just corrected. It is not part of this treatment.
distractorExplanations.c: He is still groggy. Oral paste is for a patient who can protect the airway, and the vein route was already used.

prompt: A 50-year-old man takes a daily beta blocker. After a bee sting he is wheezing, flushed, and hypotensive. A partner says to skip epinephrine because of that pill. What is the drug decision?

options.text: Skip epinephrine and give only an oral antihistamine
Give nitroglycerin so the low pressure will come back up
Wait ten minutes to see whether the beta blocker wears off
Still give intramuscular epinephrine for the anaphylaxis

explanation: Anaphylaxis with wheeze and low pressure still gets intramuscular epinephrine, including when the patient takes a beta blocker. The blocker may blunt the response, which is a reason to be ready to reassess and to involve medical control, not a reason to withhold the drug. An antihistamine alone, nitroglycerin, or a ten-minute wait does not treat this shock.

distractorExplanations.a: An oral antihistamine does not replace epinephrine when the pressure is down and the lungs are tight.
distractorExplanations.b: Nitroglycerin lowers blood pressure. This patient is already hypotensive.
distractorExplanations.c: A beta blocker does not wear off in ten minutes, and anaphylaxis should not be watched without epinephrine.

prompt: A sweaty, confused man with diabetes stands in his kitchen and can describe the weakness, but nobody knows his pill list, his drug allergies, or whether he ate breakfast, and those gaps would change what you give him. What history is still missing?

options.text: Signs and symptoms, allergies, medicines, past history, last intake, and events
Oxygen saturation, airway status, medicines, pulse, consciousness, and a heart tracing
Scene security, allergies, mechanism, pulse, last meal, and a full-body exposure
Signs and symptoms, a bedside assessment, medicines, pertinent negatives, last vitals, and events

explanation: The blanks that would change treatment in this kitchen are the medicines he takes, the drugs he cannot have, and whether he has eaten. Those sit in the history taken on a medical call, along with the symptom story, past illness, and what led up to the weakness. A monitor strip and a trauma exposure answer different questions and would not fill those blanks.

distractorExplanations.b: Saturation, airway status, pulse, consciousness, and a tracing are monitoring steps. They leave out allergies and breakfast, which change what you can give him.
distractorExplanations.c: Scene security, mechanism, and exposure belong to size-up. They do not collect the pill list and the missed meal that are missing on this call.
distractorExplanations.d: A bedside assessment, pertinent negatives, and last vitals are charting habits. They swap out allergies, past history, and last intake, which are the actual gaps.

prompt: After slipping in a grocery aisle, a woman reports severe pain high in the belly. Her companion wants the head-to-toe finished before anyone asks when the pain started, what it feels like, or where it goes. What do you need to learn about that pain?

options.text: Hazards in the aisle and a count of every other injured shopper nearby
How the pain started, what changes it, its quality, spread, score, and duration
Prior surgeries, chronic illnesses, and every medication allergy in her clinic chart
Whether she is awake and can name the store, the weekday, and why you came

explanation: Belly pain after a slip can be trauma, a visceral problem, or both, and a body survey alone cannot separate them. The history of the pain itself is a different task from aisle hazards, from old chart entries, and from whether she knows where she is. Without that symptom profile you will treat the fall and miss the complaint she is actually having.

distractorExplanations.a: Hazards and a count of shoppers are scene size-up. They do not describe when the belly pain started or where it travels.
distractorExplanations.c: Surgeries, chronic illness, and allergies are past history. They are not a profile of this pain, which is what her companion is trying to skip.
distractorExplanations.d: Naming the store and the day scores alertness. That check does not capture quality, spread, or timing of the belly pain.

prompt: A 72-year-old man suddenly cannot lift his left arm, the same side of his mouth sags, and his words come out slurred. He stays awake. Family members ask if they should wait in the living room, offer a chewable tablet, or walk him down the hall. What do you do with him?

options.text: Stay in the living room until the sagging mouth and slurred words fade
Have him chew and swallow a tablet before anyone moves him to the ambulance
Transport promptly to a hospital that can image and treat stroke
Walk him the length of the hall so you can grade his balance and coordination

explanation: One-sided weakness and slurred speech that started suddenly are time-critical. Minutes spent waiting for the face to recover, a swallowed tablet, or a walking test delay brain imaging and add a fall or choking risk. He needs a hospital that can scan and treat stroke, and the clock started when the arm failed.

distractorExplanations.a: Waiting in the living room for the droop to fade burns the window for stroke treatment, and the deficit can worsen while you watch.
distractorExplanations.b: A swallowed tablet can be dangerous if the brain bleed is the cause, and slurred speech means he may choke on it.
distractorExplanations.d: A hallway walk tests balance by risking a fall, and it postpones the trip to a hospital that can image the brain.

prompt: Sitting on a bench, a man speaks in short sentences and clutches his shirt. His radial pulse is strong at 92 beats per minute. A bystander has powered up a defibrillator and wants to deliver a shock right now. When is that shock the right treatment?

options.text: When the pulse is slow and he is dizzy but still awake and talking
When the rhythm is ventricular fibrillation or pulseless ventricular tachycardia
When chest pressure is severe but a radial pulse remains easy to feel at the wrist
When a monitored flat line is already confirmed and no shock has been delivered yet

explanation: A defibrillator shock exists to stop a heart that is quivering or racing with no output you can feel. This man is talking and has a strong radial pulse, so he is not in that state. A slow pulse while he is still awake, and a flat line on a monitor, are also not rhythms that shock is built to fix.

distractorExplanations.a: A slow pulse with dizziness still means there is a pulse. Defibrillation is not the treatment for bradycardia in someone who is awake.
distractorExplanations.c: Severe chest pressure with a radial pulse is a perfusing patient. Attaching a defibrillator to shock him treats the wrong problem.
distractorExplanations.d: A confirmed flat line is not a shockable rhythm. A shock does not restart a heart that has no electrical activity.

prompt: A guard pushing on the chest of a pulseless man on a hard floor asks how far the breastbone should move and whether the chest wall ought to spring all the way back between pushes. What depth and recoil do you coach?

options.text: About 1 inch (2.5 cm), using that same shallow push on every adult
At least 3 inches (7.5 cm), and deeper still if the rescuer feels strong
At least 2 inches (5 cm), letting the chest fully recoil
About one-half the front-to-back depth of this man's chest wall

explanation: The adult breastbone has to move about 5 cm to squeeze the heart, then spring all the way back so the chest can refill. A 2.5 cm push does not move enough blood. Pushing to 7.5 cm raises the chance of injury, and half the depth of the chest is not the adult target. Recoil is part of the same coaching point, not a separate optional step.

distractorExplanations.a: One inch, about 2.5 cm, is too shallow to circulate blood in an adult, even if the rate of pushing looks busy.
distractorExplanations.b: Three inches, about 7.5 cm, is past the adult limit. Depth beyond about 6 cm increases injury without better flow.
distractorExplanations.d: Half the front-to-back chest is too deep for an adult. A fraction of chest depth is a pediatric idea, and one-half is the wrong fraction.

prompt: In a hotel lobby a defibrillator has just fired once into a pulseless woman, and the voice prompt goes quiet. A coworker reaches for a long check of the neck before any hands return to the breastbone. What do you do instead?

options.text: Feel along the neck for a full minute before any compressions start again
Have the device analyze the rhythm again before a hand returns to the chest
Use a carotid check of up to 10 seconds before you decide on compressions
Compress again for about 2 minutes, then let the device analyze

explanation: The energy has already been delivered. Flow comes back from hands on the chest, not from a long search of the neck and not from another analysis that delays those compressions. The device asks for a rhythm check after about two minutes of CPR. A ten-second pulse limit is for the first decision about arrest, not a pause after a shock.

distractorExplanations.a: A full minute feeling the neck is a long time with no circulation. The shock does not earn a pause of that length.
distractorExplanations.b: Analyzing again immediately stacks another hands-off gap onto the shock pause. Compressions resume before the next analysis.
distractorExplanations.c: Ten seconds is the cap on the initial pulse check. Using that cap after a shock still delays compressions the guidelines want restarted at once.

prompt: A man who has lived for years with a weak heart is more tired than he was last month. You are trying to tell whether the extra fluid is in the lungs or in the veins of the body. Which finding fits the right side?

options.text: Swollen ankles and neck veins that stay filled while he sits upright
Wet sounds in both lungs and pink frothy sputum at the lips
One calf that is swollen, warm, and tender over a deep vein
A need for several pillows at night and sudden gasping that wakes him

explanation: When the right side cannot send blood forward into the lungs, pressure backs up into the veins of the body, and the lung fields can stay relatively clear. Fluid heard in the lungs, a single hot calf, and waking up gasping point somewhere else: left-sided backup, a clot in the leg, and nighttime pulmonary congestion.

distractorExplanations.b: Wet lungs and pink frothy sputum are fluid in the air spaces, the backup pattern of a left side that cannot empty.
distractorExplanations.c: One warm, tender, swollen calf is a deep-vein clot until proven otherwise, not the dependent swelling of right-sided backup.
distractorExplanations.d: Needing extra pillows and waking with a gasp are pulmonary congestion. That pattern belongs to the left side, including at night.

prompt: An unresponsive man lies on his couch with a left ventricular assist device. The controller is lit and humming, and a driveline leaves the abdomen. You cannot feel a pulse at the wrist or the neck. What do you do about the pump and the missing pulse?

options.text: Treat the missing pulse as death and end the resuscitation attempt
Place defibrillator pads directly on the driveline where it exits the skin
Follow the device protocol and call the assist-device coordinator
Unplug the controller batteries so the alarm stops and the pump can reset

explanation: Continuous-flow pumps often leave no pulse you can feel even while the controller hums and the brain is still perfused, so a missing pulse is not proof of death. Pads on the cable and pulling the batteries can stop the only forward flow he has. The coordinator and the device's own trouble steps decide whether this is a pump fault or a true arrest.

distractorExplanations.a: No palpable pulse is common with a continuous-flow pump. Ending the attempt on that finding alone treats a living patient as dead.
distractorExplanations.b: Pads go on the chest, away from the driveline. Energy delivered through the cable can burn it and stop the pump.
distractorExplanations.d: Unplugging the batteries cuts power to the pump. Alarms are handled with the coordinator, and the controller stays connected.

prompt: For two days a teenager with type 1 diabetes has urinated constantly. Her breathing is now deep and rapid, her skin is dry, and her breath smells sweet. Her mother blames a skipped lunch and a sugar that fell too low. What explains the deep breathing, the sweet odor, and two days of urination?

options.text: A rapid fall in sugar from the skipped lunch, which should leave the skin cool and sweaty
Rapid breathing caused by panic, with no acid buildup behind the deep breaths
Fluid loss after an evening of alcohol, which would fully explain the sweet odor
Diabetic ketoacidosis, with acid from ketones and heavy fluid loss

explanation: Two days of constant urination, deep rapid breathing, dry skin, and a sweet odor mean she is blowing off acid and wasting water as ketones build. A low sugar from a missed meal comes on fast and leaves the skin cool and sweaty, which is not this picture. Panic breathing and alcohol do not add days of urination in type 1 diabetes.

distractorExplanations.a: Low sugar starts quickly and makes the skin pale, cool, and sweaty. It does not cause days of heavy urination with dry skin and sweet breath.
distractorExplanations.b: Panic can speed the breathing, but it does not make the breath sweet or explain two days of constant urination in diabetes.
distractorExplanations.c: Alcohol can change the odor of the breath and dry a person out. It does not produce ketone-driven deep breathing after days of polyuria.

prompt: On the break-room floor a man's jaw is locked and his arms and legs jerk in a generalized convulsion. Coworkers move to pin his limbs, wedge a wallet between his teeth, and pour juice toward his mouth. How do you handle the convulsion?

options.text: Pin both arms and both legs hard until every jerk has fully stopped
